#4537. Here are the best electric bikes you can buy at every price level in November 2026

I’ve spent countless hours here at Electrek doing detailed hands-on testing of hundreds of electric bikes. Through thousands of miles of riding, I’ve been fortunate to learn these e-bikes inside and out, top to bottom and front to back. That long-term experience with real-world e-bike testing has helped me find the best electric bicycles on the market for just about any budget.

Below are some of the top e-bikes I’ve hand-tested for every price range, current as of November 2026. These are probably the best deals you’ll find all year on electric bikes, meaning this is the best time ever to get a new model! Check out the awesome e-bikes below, any one of which could become your next electric bike.

This list is divided into several price ranges. We’ll start with the best e-bikes under $1,000, then move on to the under-$2,000 category, under-$3,000 category, etc. The goal is to highlight some of my favorite models in various budget ranges to help you make the right decision based on your needs and budget.

The sub-$1,000 electric bike category is critical for a few reasons.

First, it’s pretty hard to produce a quality e-bike and sell it for under $1k. Most of the options in this price category make too many sacrifices in quality or longevity to earn a spot on this list as one of “the best.”

Second, many newly curious e-bike buyers just aren’t prepared to drop several thousand dollars on a brand-new concept, making this price range critical for many new e-bike shoppers.

Fortunately, we’ve found some excellent options for cheap electric bikes that can still save you some serious dough.

The Lectric XP LITE 3.0 was recently updated and is now quite likely the king of bang-for-your-buck electric bikes.

For a while now, the $999 Lectric XP 4 has reigned supreme in the budget electric bike category. That’s still a great bike, and we’ll discuss it next, but the more affordable $799 Lectric XP LITE3 is an even more wallet-friendly electric bike.

That new e-bike offers some great riding at under 800 bucks.

It’s a throttle-enabled Class 2 folding electric bike with 20″ wheels, a max speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), and a motor rated for 300W continuous and 819W peak. It’s not going to be the strongest hill climber in this list, but it does get going quickly on flat and modestly hilly terrain.

And the biggest features include quality hydraulic disc brakes, color LCD screen, turn signals, and even an optional Gates carbon belt drive system for an extra $100. Riders can also opt for a nearly double-sized battery for an extra $200.

This is the only e-bike in this price range that I know of with a 48V electrical system. All the other budget e-bikes under $800 use a 36V system and thus suffer from weaker power.

There are some things that you give up with this model, such as that the fenders aren’t included free. But for just $799, you’re still getting built-in lights, a hidden battery, large color LCD display and a lightweight folder. Plus it comes in lots of fun color options.

The Lectric XP4 is the undisputed best-selling electric bike in the US. The bike has racked up massive sales figures as riders flock to its extreme bang-for-your-buck. Simply put, it’s hard to find any other e-bike that offers this level of value!

The XP4 can get riders up to 28 mph (45 km/h) and now comes in either a 500W or 750W version, with respective battery sizes of 48V 10.4Ah and 48V 17.5Ah. The long-range version’s premium price tag ($1,299 vs the standard range model at $999) is perhaps even higher value than the already impressive base model.

Other upgrades include a new stronger rack design, torque sensor for smoother pedal assist, and improved hardware like the 8-speed transmission, hydraulic disc brakes, updated urban/trail hybrid-style tire tread, and a beautiful new TFT color screen.

The XP4 is hands-down the highest value e-bike I’ve ever tested and it’s quite obvious just how much time and effort went into building such a potent e-bike designed to fit so many different riders and tasks.

It’s hard to find a better combination of low cost and high performance anywhere in the e-bike market right now.

When Ride1Up launched the original Portola, it was pretty obvious what the game plan was: fire a shot across Lectric Ebike’s bow with a direct competitor to the Lectric XP line. By all accounts, Ride1Up nailed it with an impressive competitor. Now the company has come back with the next generation of the bike, this time attempting to take on both the XP line and XP Lite from Lectric. That’s thanks to two models, the Portola 02, and the stripped-down Portola 02 Lite.

The Ride1Up Portola 02 has a lot more going for it than just the attractive starting price of $895 for the Lite or $995 for the full-size bike with frame-integrated rack. The models offer great performance with a maximum speed of 28 mph (45 km/h) and good quality components including hydraulic disc brakes, torque sensor, front suspension, a built-in rear rack (except for the Lite), and a 750W motor.

There are two battery options available, either a 48V 10Ah or a 48V 15Ah, and the larger battery only costs an extra $100, so it’s quite worth the extra 50% range.

I love the sleek-looking frame and apparently, I’m not alone. Those who are on the hunt for a good-looking folding fat tire e-bike that doesn’t break the bank will likely find this to be one of the more fashionable options.

Once you bump up above the $1,000 limit, you start to see many more great options for e-bikes in a wide range of categories.

From electric cargo bikes to cruisers and even electric mopeds, there’s something for everyone in this price range.

The $1,249 JackRabbit OG2 is in one of these fuzzy areas between e-bikes and other e-rideables. In this case, it straddles the line between an electric bike and an electric scooter.

It more or less feels like an electric bike based on its ride geometry. However, the lack of pedals means that it could also be classified as an electric scooter, albeit a large-wheeled e-scooter.

But with those 20-inch wheels and bicycle seat, the JackRabbit OG2 rides much more like a small folding e-bike than an e-scooter. And its electronics match that of a light e-bike, too.

The 300W motor gets the little runabout up to 20 mph (32 km/h). The small 158 Wh battery only offers around 10 miles (approximately 16 km) of range, but is also conveniently small enough to easily keep a spare battery in a cargo pocket or even a small purse.

The biggest benefit of the JackRabbit is that it is so simple that the lack of frills keeps the weight down to just 25 lb (11.3 kg)! For an e-bike, that’s almost so light that it floats.

The company also released a higher power and larger battery capacity version too, which might be good for riders who want to push harder and go farther. For those that want to see a few more upgrades on this minimalist e-bike, the JackRabbit OG2 and XG might be more your size.

See my full review of the JackRabbit OG2 here.

We called the Lectric XPedition e-cargo bike a runaway success right from the start, and that’s exactly what it turned into. Now with the new Lectric XPedition 2.0 on the road, it’s better than ever.

With heavy-hauling weight capacity, the option for one or two batteries for extra long range, hydraulic disc brakes and torque sensor-based intuitive feeling pedal assist, this e-bike is dragging electric cargo bikes into the future.

The $1,399 Lectric XPedition 2.0 has turned the electric cargo bike market upside down, bringing a heavy-hitting cargo e-bike to market for an ultra-affordable price.

While it’s not the fanciest cargo e-bike on the market (you’ll find those in the $4,000-$6,000 price range further down this article), it’s definitely the best bang for your buck thanks to a combination of high value parts and reasonable pricing.

The Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is probably one of the best deals in full-suspension folding e-bikes right now. With a combination of a powerful motor, comfortable geometry, front & rear suspension, and a high-tech interface that includes NFC card unlocking, the Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is punching above its weight class.

In fact, that’s its main drawback, its weight. It’s a heavy bike, but the speed and power mean heavier motors and batteries, so you know you’re going to be carrying a more robust powertrain around with you.

But between the performance and the looks, this is one awesome comfortable ride that just doesn’t break the bank! I had a blast reviewing it, and I’ll bet you’ll have a blast riding it!

The $1,399 Aventon Soltera.2 is the latest version of Aventon’s beautiful city bike that offers some of the best quality fabrication that I’ve seen in this price range – or even in higher price ranges. It is offered in either a single-speed or seven-speed format.

The bike rolls on narrow tires for that efficient city ride, while still packing in a 500W motor.

The battery is a bit smaller at 36V and 10Ah, but the bike makes up for a smaller battery by being able to integrate it into the frame in a sleek and attractive package.

The beautiful color display also adds to the bike’s charm, as do the powerful headlight and frame-integrated tail light. There’s even an awesome companion app that lets your phone track your bike’s important stats. Basically, you’re getting a lot for $1,199 here!

Check out my in-depth Aventon Soltera.2 review here.

Ride1Up has proven itself as a high-value electric bike brand, focusing largely on efficient and speedy commuter e-bikes. While the company has many models in the $1,000 to $2,000 range, the $1,295 Ride1Up Roadster V3 is one of the best bang-for-your-buck options in the lightweight category.

This 500W-rated e-bike offers Class 3 performance, meaning you can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), or a still impressive 20 mph (32 km/h) if using the throttle. But sticking to pedal-assist means you get to enjoy that quality torque sensor for smoother pedaling. The bike even comes with an option for either a belt drive or a 10-speed Shimano transmission, and three frame sizes to choose from.

The V3’s design was updated with many new features, including a now-removable battery for even more convenient charging both on and off the bike. And with a sub-40 lb weight, it’s hard to beat this one on a pound-for-pound basis!

Check out my full review of the Ride1Up Roadster V3 here:

Lectric Ebikes expanded into larger territory with the launch of the Lectric XPeak2. It was the company’s first e-bike with a larger than 20″ wheel size, bringing some chunky 26×4.0″ tires into the company’s inventory.

The XPeak takes the form of a typical adventure-style fat tire electric bike. It features a hardtail design with a suspension fork, high-volume tires, hydraulic disc brakes, and a relatively large battery that is certified by the Swiss testing agency SGS to meet UL 2849 standards.

The bike is also tested to higher standards for ruggedness of the frame and fork than most e-bikes in this price range, meaning it’s likely going to last longer too. As far as fat tire adventure-style e-bikes go, there’s no better bang for your buck than the Lectric XPeak2.

The $2,295 Ride1Up Prodigy V2 Eco has brought new meaning to the phrase “low-cost mid-drive electric bike”, updating an already impressive e-bike with a new next-gen setup.

This e-bike sports a high-end German-manufactured Brose mid-drive motor and can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), yet is price similarly to much cheaper hub motor-based electric bikes.

It’s a perfect commuter e-bike for someone who wants high-quality parts like that German mid-drive motor with 90Nm of torque, hydraulic disc brakes, bright LED lights, included fenders, rear rack, and a very comfortable saddle. Plus, there’s a choice between a step-over or a mid-step frame to better fit a wider variety of riders.

This e-bike is easily worth another $700 more than the price tag, if not more. In fact, you’ll find many of these same components on e-bikes with $2,000-$3,000 price tags all over the place. So if you’re looking for a higher quality e-bike that doesn’t cost as much as a fancy bike shop e-bike, this is the one to consider.

The Ride1Up Vorsa is Ride1Up’s most versatile “SUV‑style” e‑bike yet, designed to transition seamlessly from commuting through city streets to loaded errands and light gravel or park paths. With a standard price around US $1,495, it delivers an exceptionally high‑value riding experience that often outperforms models far above its price range.

With a powerful 750 W rear‑hub motor producing a hefty 95 Nm of torque (and peaking over 1,400 W in real-world tests), the Vorsa accelerates comfortably and can maintain Class 3 speeds of up to 28 mph via pedal assist or 20 mph throttle thanks to its dual-sensor system and customizable display. Whether you’re hauling cargo or cruising commute lanes, the Vorsa delivers smooth, responsive power that feels natural and planted.

I love how well‑rounded the package is. Ride1Up outfits the Vorsa with a 100 mm suspension fork, comfortable ergonomic bars, multiple colors/frame styles (step‑thru or standard), and a modular rear rack rated for 440 lb total payload, which is expandable via Connect+ accessories. Hydraulic disc brakes, full fenders, integrated lighting, and passive features like UL‑certified batteries and Apple FindMy integration round out the build.

At just $1,695, the Ride1Up Vorsa is priced way below fair market value, which makes this an absolute steal of a deal.

Check out my Ride1Up Vorsa review here, and also check out the new expansion to the Vorsa line with lighter and heavier duty models built on the Vorsa platform.

The Marker is the first model unveiled by the e-bike brand spun out of Lectric eBikes, known as Monarc. The brand leverages Lectric’s size and buying power to bring higher end bikes than we typically see in the budget space – complete with higher shelf components – but at better prices and with better customer service.

The Monarc Marker is a powerful, Class 3-capable fat tire adventure e-bike with powerful four-piston brakes, a quality reverse arch suspension fork, Shimano CUES transmission, and comes with two batteries, all for an incredible reasonable MSRP of US $1,999.

Monarc also made waves by offering a 5-year warranty as well as 12-hour customer service five days a week, ensuring customers feel comfortable knowing they are buying from a company that will stick around to support riders long after the purchase is complete.

Learn more about the Monarc Marker here, or check out its current sale price here.

When Juiced returned with a vengeance after being saved by Lectric, the brand did so with two impressive new Scrambler models: a hard tail and a full-suspension bike. They’re both awesome moped-style e-bikes and handle great, but the full-suspension version definitely kicks things up a notch and allows for even wilder riding.

But since they share the same features and performance outside the rear suspension, either would make an awesome addition to your e-bike fleet. Basically, it’s a powerful yet street-legal e-bike that is designed for real-world riding, thanks in no small part to its designer, Austin Homes, being a seasoned competitive bike racer across multiple disciplines and bringing that keen eye to the Scrambler’s development.

By the time you surpass the $2,000 mark, you’re starting to get into serious e-bikes with serious performance or build quality.

If you’re spending this much, you’ll want to ensure you’re buying from a reputable company with top-notch products and service.

The Ride1Up TraiRush is the first actually quite good electric mountain bike that comes in at a budget price. It gives you a real German-made Brose motor, which offers good power matched with whisper-quiet performance. You get a dropper seat post and Maxxis Minion tires, Tektro Orion quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and a 120mm Rockshox Judy Silver TK Air Fork.

The first time I took a ride on the Ride1Up TrailRush, I couldn’t believe just how good the bike felt, especially from a company known for its wide array of commuter and street-oriented electric bikes. But Ride1Up was founded by cyclists at heart, and so they know what it means to build a good bike, regardless of category. At $2,095, this is a steal for just great parts.

I love the $3,299 Priority Current electric bike so much that it has become one of my daily riders. It’s the one I grab when I’m doing city riding and I know I want to be pedaling.

While the original version was already a great bike, the new Current Plus adds some key improvements, such as an included throttle and a nearly 50% larger capacity battery for more range. The throttle is great in a pinch, but the bike is also just so much fun to pedal thanks to a torque sensor-based pedal assist that provides natural-feeling assistance up to a fast 28 mph top speed.

The internally geared rear hub combined with a Gates belt drive system and powerful hydraulic disc brakes make this a very nice e-bike for the price. Plus that mid-drive motor offers tons of torque (140 Nm!) for climbing hills or accelerating quickly.

I’m also a fan of the built-in lights and included fenders, not to mention the punchy hydraulic disc brakes and Goodyear tires.

Mid-drive electric bikes aren’t cheap, but the price is definitely a fair one for this e-bike.

I’m not normally a carbon fiber, drop bar, race bike kind of guy. But then again, that’s usually because those types of bikes are way out of my price range… until now.

The Ride1Up CF Racer1 brings carbon fiber road e-bikes to the common man, offering both a traditional road bike and a gravel bike edition.

At under 29 lb (13 kg), these e-bikes are some of the lightest around. I picked one up with my index finger and was shocked at how easily it left the ground.

To get there, that meant a relatively low-power motor and a smaller battery were required. But for the folks that ride these types of bikes, a big motor and heavy battery probably aren’t on their wishlist anyway. Instead, a simple extra boost, as if you’ve always got a tailwind, helps augment your own pedaling.

For just $2,295, there’s no better deal out there for a budget-friendly carbon fiber road e-bike.

This full-suspension electric moped-style e-bike is a masterclass in high performance electric bike design. Sure, it’s an obvious SUPER73 imitation, but it’s a really well done imitation.

It handles well, it’s got great rubber between you and the road, the suspension gives a comfortable ride, and it’s got plenty of extra power.

Despite the 750W label, the e-bike can be unlocked to make use of nearly 1,500W of peak power. I was able to reach a top speed of 37 mph (59.5 km/h) during my testing (not on public streets!).

But the bike ships in Class 2 mode with a 750W limit and 20 mph (32 km/h) maximum speed, meaning you’ll have to contact the company to request an unlock for the bike to be used above Class 2 speeds and power levels.

All in all, the $2,395 Ride1Up REVV1 FS is an amazing e-bike for anyone who wants a moped-style ride with full-suspension, high quality 4-piston hydraulic disc brakes and a design that rides almost like a motorcycle, yet in a bike form factor.

Check out my complete Ride1Up REVV1 FS review here.

The Tern Quick Haul is an electric cargo bike from the famed cargo e-bike company Tern. It holds the distinction of being the most affordable model in Tern’s lineup.

That says a lot, because Tern is known for its high-quality e-bikes that are built to be ridden every day for real-world errands, carpool duty, and more. These e-bikes are meant to replace cars, and they do just that for many riders. With a huge list of accessories, you can outfit a Quick Haul for just about any job.

The Tern Quick Haul features a mid-drive Bosch motor, hydraulic disc brakes, Tern’s vertical parking rack, and a relatively lightweight but high utility design that is meant to carry just about anything in your life.

We had the chance to test a pair of Quick Hauls at Eurobike in Frankfurt last year, which you can learn more about here.

Motor: Bosch Active Line Plus mid-drive motorTop speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) with pedal assist (no throttle)Range: Up to 60 miles (96 km), less when riding in highest powerBattery: 400Wh, removable/lockableWeight: 50 lb (22.8 kg)Price: $2,999

When it comes to fast, powerful electric mopeds on a budget, it’s hard to compete with the $2,399 Ariel Rider X-Class. This is the e-bike I usually recommend when someone simply wants the most power and speed for the least amount of money.

The impressive performance comes from a powerful 1,000W motor that actually puts out closer to 2,000W of peak power. It can be limited to 20 mph if you’d like, but I got it up to 36 mph in unlimited mode.

The bike rolls on 20″ moto-style wheels and comes with nice parts including hydraulic disc brakes, a bench seat, dual suspension, and a big moto-style headlight.

You can see my full review of the Ariel Rider 52V X-Class here.

The Xtracycle Hopper is something of a Goldilocks cargo bike, in my opinion. It’s not as big as a traditional long tail cargo bike, but it’s still big enough to carry multiple kids or a week’s worth of groceries.

It’s also not as pricey as the expensive $5-7k bike shop cargo e-bikes, yet it’s much higher quality than the typical direct-to-consumer cargo e-bikes.

I’ve tested it for all sorts of cargo jobs and even put my friends and family on it to take their kids to school and let me know how it works for them. Everyone has come away impressed with the ride feel, which seems much more like a traditional bike than a bulky cargo bike.

For the money, the Xtracycle Hopper offers incredible value and much higher quality construction than you’d get with entry-level brands.

Check out my full Xtracycle Hopper review here.

Above $3.5k, you’re entering some seriously dedicated e-bike territory.

These e-bikes either feature top-shelf components like drivetrain and brake parts, or pack in so much power that they couldn’t possibly be priced any lower.

Either way, you’re not in Kansas anymore. You’re heading down the e-bike rabbit hole.

Tern is renowned for building high-quality electric bikes that double down on utility features. The newly updated Tern HSD is the company’s more affordable utility e-bike, offering many features you’ll find on its higher-end GSD but at a price that more riders can stomach.

The HSD uses small 20″ wheels and includes a folding stem, making it nice and compact. But taking it one step further, Tern outfitted it with its innovative rack that lets you park the bike on its tail, meaning it takes up barely more space than a coat rack in the corner of a room.

The bike’s Bosch mid-drive and high capacity batteries provide a high-end e-bike drive, and they are matched with a variety of performance drivetrain options that you can select from, depending on how high you want to spec the bike.

Whether you’re ferrying around kids or buying a week’s worth of groceries, the HSD is a solid option.

Check out my detailed first ride experience on the Tern HSD here.

The Xtracycle Swoop ASM is one of those electric cargo bikes that makes you rethink the entire category.

Not only does it include high-quality components and fancy features like automatic shifting paired with a high-end Shimano mid-drive motor, but it also just feels like you’re riding a normal-sized bike instead of a long and awkward cargo e-bike.

I found I can even ride it without my hands on the bars because it tracks so straight and rides so stable. That’s a feat you can’t pull off with most budget cargo e-bikes since they aren’t designed with proper bicycle geometry. But Xtracycle is a true cyclist’s cargo e-bike company, and so they understand proper bicycle design.

Check out my full review of this incredibly high-end and comfortable-to-ride cargo e-bike here.

When it comes to all-wheel-drive electric bikes, the $3,299 Ariel Rider Grizzly is one of my favorites.

This incredible e-bike is really more of a small electric motorcycle. It uses two high-power motors – one in each wheel – to offer speeds in the mid-30s and acceleration that will get you there in the blink of an eye.

Full suspension and hydraulic disc brakes make this an e-bike that handles well at any speed, and the bright red paint job looks as aggressive as the e-bike feels. It even comes with footpegs pre-installed so you can carry a passenger with you.

Plus it’s got double batteries to feed those two power-hungry motors, so you’ll be able to ride this e-bike pretty darn far too, as long as you aren’t too demanding from the throttle.

Check out my full in-depth review of the epic Ariel Rider Grizzly e-bike here.

The Priority Skyline builds upon Priority Bicycles’ legacy of creating high-performance, low-maintenance e-bikes and ups the ante with more premium parts than we’ve ever seen on a Priority e-bike before.

The show stopper here is the inclusion of Pinion’s 12-speed automatic gearbox, which smartly shifts gears without the rider ever having to think about it. You can personalize your shift points to dial in the ride, and let the centrally-mounted gearbox do the rest. The carbon belt drive transfers your pedal power while a 750W rear hub motor brings the extra power riders need.

There are also high-quality hydraulic brakes, a great suspension fork, and a big battery for long range in the city. Rear rack and complete fenders come standard, as do the built-in LED lights and adjustable handle-bar stem.

See my full review of the Priority Bicycles Skyline here.

You just couldn’t stop, could you? I showed you plenty of awesome e-bikes that didn’t cost most of a paycheck. But you just haaaaaaad to keep going.

Fine, here they are. These are some of the most expensive e-bikes out there that we’ve tested and that I’d actually recommend someone buying, if you can pony up the cash.

When it comes to ultra-premium folding electric bikes, there’s only one name that comes to my mind: GoCycle. These are the most impressive folding e-bikes I’ve ever seen. And they better be – they were designed by a former McLaren engineer.

Between the carbon fiber work, single-sided wheels, high-tech tires, trippy LED dot display, innovative rear suspension, and completely enclosed drivetrain, there’s a lot of high-end stuff going on here.

The speed will vary from 15-20 mph depending on which country you buy the bike in, but the performance is only part of the equation. The quick folding and light, compact design of the e-bike is the real winner here.

Check out my full review of the GoCycle G4i+ here.

The FREY EX Pro is a high-end electric mountain bike with crazy high power. It uses the same motor as the CSC FT1000MD we featured above (the Bafang M620 mid-drive), but cranks up the current to provide closer to 1,500W of power.

It’s enough to destroy chains if you aren’t careful. We know. Several of us here at Electrek have done it.

The FREY EX Pro not only features high-end parts like a RockShox Lyric fork and Magura MT5e hydraulic brakes, but it even comes with dual batteries so you can ride farther and stay on the trails longer.

I’ve personally taken this e-bike back UP a downhill mountain bike course – that’s how powerful it is.

It may be expensive, but it saves you several thousand dollars compared to many European electric mountain bikes with similar components but a fraction of the power in the FREY.

See my full review of the FREY EX Pro here.

The Tern GSD improves upon the Tern HSD with even more capability and even nicer components. There are multiple versions that can take you up to nearly $10k, but even the lower-tier versions are not “low tier,” if you know what I mean.

Parts like automatically engaging electric locks, 10-speed Shimano Deore transmissions, Magura MT5e quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and more set these e-bikes apart from the rest of the pack.

If you’re getting a Tern GSD, you’re getting a fully qualified car replacement. There are many people who use these instead of buying a second car. When you look at it like that, the price suddenly seems pretty reasonable.

Check out our full review of the Tern GSD here.

#4536. High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Shows

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.

The researchers from Arizona State University said a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.

The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.

The researchers published their findings on November 12 in the journal Stem Cell Reports.

The researchers said the study is important because 1 in 25 people develop colon cancer in their lifetime. In the United States, that translates into about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer every year. About 55,000 males and 55,000 females are expected to die from the disease in 2026.

Experts not involved in the study say the research provides valuable information, but they have reservations about the results, as the findings do not yet apply to humans.

“The findings provide a potential mechanism linking diet to intestinal cancer development, but we need to be cautious about translating these results to humans,” said Dalia Perelman, MS, CDE, a research dietitian at Stanford University in California.

“We already have evidence from human studies that obesity and certain dietary patterns, particularly those high in processed meats and low in fiber-rich foods, are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk,” Perelman told Healthline. “This study adds a potentially important mechanism to investigate, but it does not establish that dietary fat itself increases colorectal cancer risk in humans.”

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, shared similar views.

“This study provides a better understanding at the cellular level of how a high fat diet may contribute to colorectal cancer development,” Thanki told Healthline.

“Animal studies are an important starting point for understanding biological processes, but we must be cautious about directly applying their findings to humans,” he added. “Mice and humans share many cellular and biological mechanisms, which makes these studies valuable in identifying potential pathways involved in disease development. However, human diets, genetics, metabolism, and environmental exposures are more complex.”

To reach their findings, the Arizona State researchers fed mice what the scientists described as a Western-style high fat diet for 6 months.

They then compared those results with those from mice given a low fat diet.

The researchers said the mice on the high fat diet gained more weight than the mice on the low-fat diet. They also developed more intestinal stem cells, and those cells grew at a more rapid rate.

They added that mice genetically predisposed to intestinal cancer who were fed a high-fat diet developed more and larger tumors.

The researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may help explain their increased growth and survival.

They also pointed out that stem cell behavior returned to normal after high fat diet mice were switched to a low fat diet, although some DNA changes persisted. After four weeks, approximately 18% of these changes remained.

When mice were returned to a high fat diet, the researchers said their intestinal stem cells responded more quickly and strongly than those of mice exposed to the diet for the first time.

They concluded that the study suggests that maintaining a healthy, low fat diet may help regulate intestinal stem cell growth and reduce colon cancer risk.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, RD, president of KAK Consulting and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Ohio, wasn’t involved in the study but highlighted a particular aspect of the findings.

“What I found particularly interesting was that even after the mice returned to a low fat diet, some of the molecular changes persisted,” she told Healthline. “This raises questions about how our dietary patterns over time may influence long-term health.”

Experts said these new findings are interesting but noted numerous caveats.

“One important takeaway is that dietary habits over time matter,” said Thanki. “Even if someone has consumed a high fat diet for years, making changes now may still provide meaningful health benefits.”

“I also think these findings are particularly important for children and adolescents, as establishing healthier dietary habits early in life may provide long-term benefits,” he added.

However, Thanki noted that not all fats are the same. “The health risks depend partly on the type of fat consumed, how much is consumed, and what foods make up the overall diet,” he said.

“Diets consistently high in saturated fats, particularly those containing large amounts of processed meats, fried foods, and highly processed products, can contribute to obesity, elevated cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction. These factors can also contribute to chronic inflammation and may increase the risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer,” Thanki continued.

Perelman said the diet used in the study was extremely high in fat, providing 60% of calories from fat, primarily from lard.

“We know that the health effects of dietary fats differ depending on their sources and fatty acid composition, and we cannot assume that a diet rich in unsaturated fats from foods such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds would produce the same effects,” she noted.

Perelman added that the researchers primarily studied stem cells from the small intestine rather than the colon.

“Although these tissues share some biological characteristics, they have important differences, and we cannot assume that the same changes would occur in the colon,” she explained.

Finally, Perelman noted that “the mice consuming the high fat diet also gained weight, making it difficult to separate the effects of dietary fat itself from those associated with increased body fat and other metabolic changes.”

Not all high fat foods are unhealthy. Some high fat foods that offer healthy benefits include:

“The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to eliminate fat because our bodies need healthy fats for normal functioning,” said Thanki. “Instead, people should focus on reducing saturated and trans fats while incorporating healthier unsaturated fats in appropriate amounts.”

Thanki had several dietary suggestions. Among them:

“Consistency matters more than perfection. Even modest dietary changes, maintained over time, can have meaningful health benefits,” Thanki said.

Perelman agreed. “The overall quality of the diet matters. Diets that are very high in fat may displace other foods and nutrients that have important health benefits,” she said.

“For colorectal cancer specifically, higher intakes of dietary fiber and whole grains have consistently been associated with lower risk,” Perelman noted.

“Therefore, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing fat, it is important to consider the overall dietary pattern and whether it provides adequate amounts of fiber-rich plant foods and other beneficial nutrients.”

Kirkpatrick agreed that the type of fat is what is important. “A Mediterranean-style diet that includes olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish can be relatively high in fat but is consistently associated with positive health outcomes,” she said.

“On the other hand, a diet high in saturated fat, processed meats, and ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of certain chronic diseases, particularly when it’s also low in fiber and other protective nutrients.”

Kirkpatrick also noted that many lifestyle habits contribute to a person’s overall health.

“Our health is influenced by so many factors beyond diet, including how we manage stress, our sleep habits, physical activity, genetics, and overall lifestyle,” she said.

#4535. Robotic slugs with claws can fuse together to create one massive machine

Published Nov 12, 2026 1:07 PM EST

An unsuspecting traveler trucking their way through a hiking trail would likely stop in bewilderment if they saw it: a nearly two-foot-long, Slinky-like contraption made of plastic and rubber, clambering forward like an inchworm. That confusion would shift to unease when scanning up and down its bendy, elephant-trunk-like body and seeing pairs of snapping claws at either end. Unabashed horror would inevitably take over as our traveler watches another one of the soulless Slinkies appear, inch toward the first one, and connect at the claws, creating one much larger, lifeless wiggly slug. All around, more clawed robots would close in from the forest and merge until they’d combined into a lizard-like mishmash of plastic and claws the size of a small bear.

These clawed robots are, in fact, real and they are the latest creation coming from the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Colorado State University. Inspired by the unique, flexible strength of elephant trunks, the 3D-printed TeCoBots robots are an attempt to work around the  usual rigid constraints of building a robot. The team used an approach called tensegrity, in which the cylindrical rods in the robot’s body are held in place by a web of tensioned cables rather than rigidly locked together. This makes it bendy, like a Slinky, so it can twist and turn around obstacles or collapse down on itself. In testing, a remote human operator was able to use the robot’s bendy body and gripper claws on either of its ends to traverse over a large branch outdoors. It can also roll over itself repeatedly, shimmy up a pipe, and slither like a snake.

But as our unfortunate hypothetical hiker discovered, TeCoBot really shines when it works with others. Engineers designed the robots so that their claws can grasp onto another robot and merge. These modular robot links can move as one or operate independently of each other to complete more complicated tasks. In the study and accompanying videos, gaggles of chained TeCoBots work together to climb up a desk and grab a pen, open a sealed jar, or grab an object and carry it across a room. All of this, the researchers emphasize, has humanity’s best interest at heart. The robot’s flexible design could make them invaluable tools in search and rescue missions where they could squeeze into places rescuers can’t reach. One day, these teams of robotic slugs may work together to accomplish tasks unsuited for humans on spacecraft and extraterrestrial planets.

“In the future, we can envision mostly autonomous teams of tens or even hundreds of them – attached through the claws—traveling to a location and then deploying for a specific purpose,” Colorado State University Associate Professor Jianguo Zhao said in a statement. “They are very adaptable to the situation and goals.”

Details of the robot were published this week in the journal Nature Machine Intelligence.

Zhao and his colleagues started the project to fill some of the gaps in current robot hardware. Though many new types of machines are being built these days, most are still made from sturdy but rigid materials that limit their flexibility. Most robots also tend to prioritize either locomotion (moving) or manipulation (grabbing stuff), with few excelling at both.

Like most human problems, nature already devised a solution long ago. In this case, the researchers looked to the remarkable combination of strength and flexibility in an elephant’s trunk. These marvels of evolution let the world’s largest land mammals both heft rocks weighing several hundred pounds and gently peel open bananas. That wide range and adaptability could come in handy for a robot.

The device they ended up creating measured one foot 11 inches long, has a 4.3-inch diameter and weighs around 600 grams (1.3 pounds) without batteries, roughly the same as a fully loaded Italian sub. Each robot module is made of six carbon fiber rods and a continuous, stretchable, 3D-printed tension. This stretchy and bendy design means one robot can bend either direction, stretch up like an accordion or collapse down on itself.

The claws at either end of TeCoBot are fundamental to how it can combine with its fellow slinky-bots. The grippers connect and lock onto each other, reducing the need for other connectors like magnets, which are more prone to mechanical failure. Once connected, each robot can offload certain physical stresses to the others to lighten its load, giving the whole system what the research team refers to as a kind of “embodied intelligence.”

Working together, these linked robots can complete far more complicated tasks than any one of them could alone. In demonstration videos, the robots roll towards each other and connect to form one long robot that can more easily loop around a pipe. In another example, several more robots combine to form an H-shape, which then allows the entity to climb along a duct. The merged robots are still able to use the unlined claws at either end to precisely grab objects. The team demonstrated this by instructing a multi-robot TeCoBot chain to climb a desk, pluck a pen out of a container with its claw, crawl back down to the ground, and drop the pen into a trash can.

“They can bend around to lift and carry different sized objects with their body or to navigate difficult terrain like a snake would,” Zhao said.

This actually isn’t the first time roboticists have turned to elephants for design choices. A previous entry called EleTac from a team out of Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology replaced the main sensors and camera normally in a robot grippers with essentially one massive integrated sensor able to “feel” an object’s texture. That approach, mirroring an elephant’s tactile trunk, resulted in a gripper that could hold a sponge and wipe down dirty plates and blindly feel for a pen buried beneath a layer of sand.

Meanwhile, another team from the University of Hong Kong,created their own Aerial Elephant Trunk robot grippers and strapped them to the sides of flying drones, essentially giving them a floppy, grippy tail. Real samples of elephant trunk skin tissue have also been studied and used as a reference point for  new surface material that could be used to make  soft robots that are similarly tough and durable on one end but flexible and sensitive on the other.

#4534. Going the distance: these electric semi trucks cover over 600 miles EVERY DAY

“Sure, diesel is high, but electric trucks don’t work.” It’s a common refrain these days – especially from people selling diesel trucks. Perception lags reality, however, and the reality is that these electric semi trucks are covering more than 600 miles per day, seven days a week.

Over the course of the last year, Hendrik Müller, managing partner of DEFRU Logistik GmbH has transformed his company’s shipping fleet, switching thirty of their HD prime movers (semi trucks) to electric power and immediately putting the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600s to work, covering 1,000 km (~620 miles) of German highways each and every day.

Benjamin Budick, a Senior Manager, Own Retail Mercedes-Benz Trucks Dortmund & Haan, took to LinkedIn to announce the successful deployment, and posted some great pictures of the handover showing the big Mercedes trucks in full DEFRU livery.

Mercedes’ eActros 600 packs a whopping, 621 kWh battery that helps the trucks cover 500 km per charge, allowing fleets to move goods between ports and regional fulfillment centers, charging along the way, or while they’re getting loaded and unloaded at their destination, all the while saving the fleet serious money – even before the latest Iran War sent diesel prices skyrocketing.

That big battery sends electrons to Mercedes-Benz’s proprietary electric drive axles, which deliver 1.61 kWh / mile efficiency while rolling out at an average of 36 metric tons (~79,400 lbs.) combined vehicle weight – specs that rivals the theoretical efficiency claims of the Tesla Semi. Except in the real world. And in winter.

The eActros is a serious beast. As mentioned there are many configurations and they seem to work well in Europe. I've seen one that was configured with 620kWh battery, on one side a MCS port plus a CCS2 port (so thats either 1.2MW or 600kW charging options) and on the other side a CCS2 port.

In Europe with CCS, 350kW chargers are easy to find, 400kW are becoming more common and 600kW models are starting to arrive, therefore with the limitations on driving hours and speeds, the eActros really is an all day every day truck.

Of course if you are in the far North of Europe and are allowed to haul 60 tonnes, Scania have made a complete monster of a truck with over 800kWh of battery!

The company recently expanded its eActros lineup to include over 40 possible configurations, giving customers a choice of two cab designs, two or three battery packs, multiple wheelbases and new axle configurations, covering everything from short-haul drayage to serious, off highway vocational work.

#4533. Dream Driving Experiences Make the Perfect Gift for Auto Enthusiasts

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Give them something they'll never forget. From budget experiences to luxury excursions, there's a dream driving experience for every driver no matter the occasion.

This article was updated in November 2026.

Auto enthusiasts are notoriously difficult to shop for. Most already have their own tools, collectibles, garage décor, and driving gadgets, and they’re very particular about all of it. They've probably spent hours researching exactly which version they want. Good luck to anyone trying to buy them something last-minute.

It stands to reason, then, that the best gift for a car lover might be an opportunity to actually get behind the wheel.

Whether it's thrashing an exotic supercar around a famous track, honing their skills through professional instruction, tackling rugged terrain in an off-roader, chasing the Northern Lights by snowmobile, wafting over Europe's greatest roads in a luxurious grand tourer, or strapping into an actual race car for a full-speed ride-along, these experiences offer something every car enthusiast longs for—more time in the seat. The vehicles may differ, but the result is the same—a memory they'll be cherishing long after the holidays have passed.

Best of all, many of these driving experiences are offered as gift certificates or gift cards, which makes them excellent for last-minute gifting. E-vouchers from gifting sites are more versatile and far more personalized—and usually way more affordable—than pricier branded experiences from manufacturers. Your favorite driver can select their own driving vacation on their own schedule at locations around the world.

Got a car lover that's hard to buy for? Here's what we recommend, any time of year.

Virgin Gifts is another gifting site that sells e-vouchers for experiences, so your favorite driver can reserve their ultimate driving experience at their convenience. It's a great last-minute gift idea.

Our pick? BMW Performance Driving Experiences at official BMW proving grounds in either Greer, South Carolina, or Thermal, California (near Palm Springs). At the M Driving School, your favorite Bimmer lover will learn how to drive the legendary M line from professional drivers. They'll slip into the driver's seat of multiple M cars and conquer low- and high-speed driving exercises such as a slalom course and autocross, as well as a wet skidpad for drifting. Once they've mastered each course, they'll compete in timed runs against other drivers. The High-Performance Driver School is the same but with a wider variety of cars and experiences. The Teen Driver School is a fantastic option for young Bimmer fans to learn the basics.

Drive with us! Road & Track Experiences offers several opportunities each year to tour and explore a variety of locales around the U.S. You and a guest will join R&T editors for luxurious and leisurely rallies. Show off your most prized vehicles to like-minded enthusiasts, all while driving legendary roads in beautiful areas, staying in top-notch hotels, and eating at the finest restaurants.

In 2027, the Palm Canyon Run will explore the California Desert in late February, from Palm Springs and Joshua Tree to track time at Chuckwalla, as desert flowers bloom and temperatures are moderate and comfortable. In May, join us for a one-of-a-kind trip through New England, including the famous Kancamagus!

Got a trip to Las Vegas planned? Get out of the casino and onto the racetrack! Give your favorite car lover the chance to drive the world’s largest and fastest selection of Lamborghinis, Ferraris, Porsches, and more at Las Vegas Motor Speedway.

Tinggly is an aggregate gifting site that offers dozens of driving experiences from reputable services all over the world. Most Tinggly gifts are offered as gift e-cards; that means your favorite car lover can choose any experience they desire anywhere they want and on their own schedule. Even if driving exotic cars on a racetrack isn't their cup of tea, there's something at Tinggly that's guaranteed to get their motor running.

If your favorite auto enthusiast has impeccable taste for the finest, Huntermoss is the ultimate gift. Huntermoss (formerly Ultimate Driving Tours) curates luxurious tours and driving experiences in exotic supercars that celebrate passion for motoring and an appreciation for the finer things in life. With experiences in Europe, North America, and Australia, it's a gift and a memory they'll always treasure.

Huntermoss offers guided and self-guided tours and weekend getaways, so there's an experience for everyone who has the means. They'll get to choose from driving a selection of supercars on the world's best roads, enjoying VIP hospitality at F1 races, or strapping into a race car to conquer iconic circuits like Nürburgring and Spa. Huntermoss also offers a bespoke travel-management service, so let your imagination run wild in creating your dream driving holiday. Lavish accommodations, gourmet dining, and handpicked lifestyle experiences complete this bucket-list journey.

If your favorite auto lover is a racing fan, VRBO offers dozens of trackside and track-adjacent rental properties around the world, including this incredible first-turn luxury condo at Charlotte Motor Speedway.

First, buy tickets to any race at StubHub for the best deals, then check out the local listings near the track at VRBO (do this well in advance to get a great deal) and book a vacation property close to or on the track.

Whether you're looking into NASCAR, MotoGP, Formula 1, or even IndyCar and IMSA races, simply book a home in Daytona, Laguna Seca, Bristol, COTA, or anywhere else through VRBO and avoid the hassle of the hotel hustle. It's way more comfortable and lets you and your friends make the most of your visit.

Giftory is another "experience gifting" site that lets you buy gift certificates for all kinds of driving experiences in hundreds of locations worldwide. The NASCAR Ride-Along Experience is available at more than 10 NASCAR racetracks in the U.S., so your favorite driver can choose a track close to home or at a legendary course such as Daytona.

Like Tinggly, Giftory offers hundreds of experiences all around the world, including dozens of driving experiences such as UTV adventures in Moab and snowmobiling excursions to see the Northern Lights.

Porsche enthusiasts will feel the thrill behind the wheel of classic and legendary Porsches at Porsche Driving Experience locations all over the U.S. Whether it's a Driver Development Course in Atlanta or Los Angeles or a Track Experience at Laguna Seca or Birmingham, there's something for every Porsche lover. There are even Travel Experiences that let your favorite Porsche driver tour with like-minded Porsche fans.

For the Porsche enthusiast who demands the best, opt for the Porsche Track Experience in Europe. Once-in-a-lifetime opportunities include introductory courses to GT track days to the top-of-the-line Rennsport Academy.

One of the most renowned driving and racing experiences in the world, Skip Barber offers one- and three-day Racing Schools behind the wheel of either a modified GT car or an FIA homologated monocoque paired with a 160-hp turbocharged four-cylinder engine at a variety of tracks all over the U.S. For experienced drivers, there are also two-day Advanced schools in both cars. (We reviewed the Skip Barber experience back in 2018, shortly after the company changed hands; you can read about that here.)

Skip Barber's renowned Driving Academy makes a great gift for drivers of all skill levels, particularly young or new drivers who need to hone their skills and tactics behind the wheel.

Just outside Phoenix, Arizona, lies one of the nation's top driving and racing schools. Radford is renowned for its top-flight educational programs, helping drivers reach their maximum potential behind the wheel.

Sponsored by Dodge, Radford offers multiple programs and experiences for drivers of all skill levels in Challengers, Hellcats, SRTs, and more, including driving and racing schools at multiple skill levels and at numerous price points—even drag racing and private instruction.

Racing's number-one oil and fluids brand also runs a marvelous racing school at locations all over the country. If your favorite auto enthusiast has racing aspirations, then this is the ultimate gift idea.

Lucas Oil School of Racing isn't intended to be a casual vacation experience or even necessarily a "fun" activity—although it certainly is that! LOSR is a serious racing school designed to develop aspiring race-car drivers, and its top graduates often move on to professional racing ladders such as IndyCar and IMSA.

With Basic, Basic+, Advanced, and Championship levels, students compete on a level field with other talented up-and-coming drivers in Ray Formula GR11 race cars. These championship-winning cars are adapted to the rigors of a racing school and arrive-and-drive race series, with an extra-large cockpit, adjustable pedal box, and adjustable seat. Courses take place year-round at tracks such as Sebring, Laguna Seca, Mid-Ohio, and VIR. See the complete 2026 calendar here.

About 40 minutes from downtown Seattle, nestled in the foothills of the Cascade Mountains, is the 315-acre DirtFish Rally School. DirtFish offers a wide range of rally driving programs that teach car control, confidence behind the wheel, and recognized rally techniques on multiple surfaces.

Outfitted with a fleet of all-wheel-drive turbocharged Subaru WRX STIs and rear-wheel-drive Subaru BRZs, DirtFish offers the excitement of rally racing to drivers with half-day, full-day, and three-day courses suitable for all drivers. Some sellers allow exchanges or let the recipient choose from a broader collection of experiences. Check the exchange policy and any price difference rules before buying; flexibility can make a specific driving gift easier to give with confidence.

Yes. A general experience voucher or collection can let the recipient choose their own activity. Tinggly, for instance, offers driving and motor experience collections, while Virgin Gifts sells specific driving experience vouchers.

Often. Many experiences offer instant email delivery, and some sellers also offer a printed voucher or gift box. Tinggly says its physical gift box includes a voucher and booking information; options vary by product.

Confirm where the experience takes place, how far the recipient would need to travel, what the voucher includes, and whether there are extra costs for booking, upgrades, or photos. Also check age and license requirements, available dates, cancellation terms, and voucher expiration.

#4531. Electric dirt bikes keep getting called e-bikes. The bicycle industry wants that to stop

The line between electric bicycles and electric motorcycles has been getting increasingly blurry – though perhaps not because the vehicles themselves are actually that hard to tell apart.

Instead, much of the confusion comes down to terminology. High-powered electric dirt bikes capable of reaching motorcycle-like speeds are increasingly being referred to as “e-bikes,” despite sharing relatively little with the low-speed electric bicycles millions of Americans use for commuting and recreation.

Now the U.S. bicycle industry is asking federal regulators to make that distinction much clearer.

PeopleForBikes, the bicycle industry’s leading trade association, recently testified before the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), calling for stronger federal regulations that specifically distinguish electric bicycles from higher-powered e-motos and electric dirt bikes.

“E-bikes and e-motos are fundamentally different products, and federal safety regulations need to reflect that distinction,” explained PeopleForBikes Policy and General Counsel Matt Moore. “When high-powered electric dirt bikes are marketed as e-bikes, it creates confusion for consumers and puts the credibility of legitimate e-bikes at risk.”

There’s a real nomenclature problem hiding underneath all of this. The term “e-bike” is widely used as shorthand for “electric bicycle,” but it isn’t exclusively used that way. Motorcycles have been called “bikes” for generations, and motorcycle media and riders will sometimes casually refer to electric motorcycles as “e-bikes” too, just in the way a biker refers to his Harley as his “bike”. In fact, it all comes from the same root. We don’t call motorcyclists “motorists”, do we? No… we call them “bikers”.

All of that makes phrases like “legal e-bike” and “legitimate e-bike” that were even used by PeopleForBikes in its arguments somewhat problematic when discussing proposed regulation. The term “e-bike” simply doesn’t mean anything specific, at least not legally.

What actually matters from a legal standpoint is whether a vehicle meets the codified definition of an electric bicycle, not whether someone calls it an e-bike – especially when the term e-bike is practically applied so broadly. In other words, perhaps part of separating electric bicycles from e-motos is being more precise with the terminology ourselves: “electric bicycle” has a specific regulatory meaning, while “e-bike” has increasingly become a much fuzzier colloquial term. As much as some would want the term “e-bike” to mean something with pedals, it simply doesn’t – at least not in North America.

I’m certainly guilty of this myself in my writing and videos, falling back on the commonly used phrasing instead of the technical legal terminology, but keeping them separated could help with the growing misunderstanding in the industry.

That distinction has become increasingly important as lightweight electric motorcycles and dirt bikes have exploded in popularity. Many feature bicycle-like frames and components, and some even include pedals, but their performance can extend far beyond what federal law defines as a low-speed electric bicycle.

The concern goes beyond mere semantics. When a 50-60 mph (80-100 km/h) electric dirt bike gets lumped into the same category as a 20-28 mph (32-45 km/h) commuter e-bike, crashes and reckless riding involving the former can quickly become part of the public conversation surrounding the latter. That can ultimately influence how lawmakers, regulators, police departments, and the general public view e-bikes as a whole.

In fact, many of the supposed electric bicycle crash figures we’ve seen touted in the news aren’t from electric bicycles at all, but rather from e-moto accidents that have been lumped in with electric bicycles, making the latter appear more dangerous than they truly are.

If street-legal electric bicycles were separated from e-motos in crash statistics, the category would be revealed to be much safer than conventional reporting would have us believe.

All of this and more has led to PeopleForBikes pushing federal regulators to draw a clearer line.

As part of its CPSC testimony, the organization recommended retaining the existing federal definition of a low-speed electric bicycle while creating a separate definition for e-motos, including machines capable of speeds up to 60 mph (96 km/h). It also called for mandatory electrical safety standards for off-road e-motos, which it says currently fall into a regulatory gap, as well as greater scrutiny of conversion kits capable of turning conventional bicycles into vehicles operating beyond their original structural design limits.

well, if its not an electric bicycle, it should be treated as a moped, registration and insurance at least, possibly a VIN and a title. So it must carry a plate if it rides on the street.

Personally I think even the level-3 electric bicycle standard (28mph with pedal assist) is to permissive, even gas mopeds have pedals, and few exceed 30mph.

But I'll lose that argument most of the time.

Now, suggestion, in the USA: a new category for "light motorcycle".

HP limit at about 15, weight limit at about 250lb(or less), speed limit at about 60, not allowed on freeways and interstates. Gas or electric does not matter. License, registration, title, insurance, they all depend on the state mostly. Helmet required, if rider is younger?

A great entry point for younger riders, much of Europe does it like this.

The testimony came as the CPSC considers new mandatory federal battery safety standards for e-bikes and other electric mobility devices. PeopleForBikes says it supports stronger battery standards, while recommending that regulators rely on existing UL standards without modification.

PeopleForBikes is also asking the CPSC and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to coordinate enforcement against e-motos that evade federal requirements.

None of this means e-motos are inherently bad. They’re incredibly fun machines, and there’s a rapidly growing market for them. But a 60 mph (96 km/h) electric dirt bike isn’t an electric bicycle simply because it looks vaguely like one.

And increasingly, the bicycle industry wants regulators to make sure everyone understands the difference.

#4530. How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight. But for those with eczema, this time of year can wreak havoc on their skin, too.

That’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s. During the winter months, she often dreads the cold.

“[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.

Cold weather and indoor heating can reduce humidity, drying out the skin and triggering or worsening eczema flare-ups.

“[What we know] about the skin barrier is that it really is like a gate or wall against the outside world,” Camille Howard-Verovic, MD, a dermatologist at Active Dermatology, told Healthline.

In healthy skin, the barrier controls what enters and leaves the skin. However, for people with eczema, Howard-Verovic said they have skin barrier dysfunction, which allows substances such as allergens and irritants to penetrate the skin.

Cold weather can increase transepidermal water loss, a process in which moisture escapes through the skin’s outer barrier and evaporates into the surrounding air.

“People with eczema have a tremendous amount of transepidermal water loss, so you’re just drier,” said Howard-Verovic. “[You’re] not holding onto the water as well, so that causes the itching and the rash that we feel when we have eczema.”

Rowland first noticed eczema flares behind her ears as well as on her elbows, arms, and the back of her knees.

“[It] looked like a rash, so that’s what I thought it was all this time, and I dealt with it for so long until after I had my son and then it started to get worse on my face,” she said.

She eventually went to a dermatologist who diagnosed her with moderate-to-severe eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that can cause intense itching, painful skin cracking, thickened skin, and redness or swelling.

When Rowland learned that eczema can be genetic, it made sense to her.

“I remember seeing big rashes on [my mom’s] neck and her arms…so she had it, and I guess I was the lucky one,” said Rowland.

At first, she tried eliminating foods that she thought might be triggers. She also bathed in oatmeal.

“[I] literally have had a tub full of oatmeal, like literally went to the store to get store-bought fresh oats,” she said. “I tried everything, and it doesn’t help until you go talk to a doctor about it.”

At first, she tried prescription topical medications but found them cumbersome.

“I don’t have the time, if I’m being honest, and we live in a world that is moving so fast…I started buying like three tubes of whatever it was I was using and losing it; it was just too much for me,” Rowland said.

Rowland said she found relief with Ebglyss, a prescription injectable medication for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. She has also partnered with Eli Lilly and Company, its manufacturer, to raise awareness about eczema.

Rowland said she’s sharing her experience to help others living with eczema, including people she’s met who have experienced greater challenges managing the condition.

“One lady was telling me about how she’s having a tough time [looking] in the mirror cause she doesn’t know who’s looking back at her, and she saw her skin before eczema and after,” said Rowland.

When she first had symptoms, she said she felt embarrassed, too.

“[Because] it was just in the middle of my arm space and…[if I] put out my hand to shake someone’s hand, you don’t know if somebody’s judgy,” she said.

Rowland hopes being open about her condition will encourage others to advocate for themselves and talk with their doctor about treatment options.

Because eczema can look different on deeper skin tones, Howard-Verovic noted that a dermatologist can help make the correct diagnosis.

“Some people may not even know that they have eczema,” she said. “We know that eczema is a rash; it can appear red on certain skin tones, and it can be grey or white on certain skin tones, so it can look a little different.”

In addition to medication, Rowland said managing stress helps reduce her eczema flare-ups.

“Before [when] I went on tour, because I was under so much stress, it flared up like crazy, like you wouldn’t believe,” she said. “We were in the back trying to figure out how to cover certain things up, and we figured some of it out, and some of it was really tricky, but what helped was when I actually just calmed down…not that it helped overnight, but it did just kind of bring the flare down.”

She said red light therapy, feeling grounded outside without her shoes on, getting vitamin D from natural sunlight, and cooking are ways she reduces ongoing stress.

“Cooking calms me when my kids aren’t here, and I have a really good [Zen] playlist on,” said Rowland. “[If] you ask me a question [in those moments], I might give you my heart; I’m just so happy.”

She also tries to cut back on sugar, which she believes triggers flares.

Another way to reduce flares, according to Howard-Verovic, is to avoid hot showers, especially in the winter.

“[We] know eczematous skin likes lukewarm water,” she said.

Because Howard-Verovic and her daughter both live with eczema, she set a rule about when it’s time to get out of the shower.

“[If] you see condensation on the bathroom mirror, you’ve spent too much time in the shower,” said Howard-Verovic. “[That] really hot, hot water feels really good in that moment…but when you get out all that water evaporates, and there’s no moisture in the atmosphere, and it dries your skin out, and now your skin is unhappy again.”

If you prefer to take baths, she said use gentle cleansers.

“[There] are bleach baths for really, really bad flare-ups,” she noted.

Diluted bleach baths are sometimes recommended for people with eczema, but they should only be used according to a healthcare professional’s instructions.

As soon as you get out of the shower or bath, Howard-Verovic said to apply a quality moisturizer to your damp skin. According to the National Eczema Association (NEA), lotions containing the following ingredients can help ease dry skin associated with eczema.

To help identify appropriate products, look for ones that have the NEA’s Seal of Acceptance.

#4529. Critically endangered tortoises slurp up pumpkin soup

Published Nov 12, 2026 2:00 PM EST

‘Tis the season for pumpkin: the “Superbowl of Pumpkin Weigh Offs,” pumpkin spice lattes, and prepping Thanksgiving feasts. One group of endangered tortoises are enjoying the season with a soup served inside a pumpkin bowl.

The trio of critically endangered Asian giant tortoises (Manouria emys phayrei) at the Turtle Survival Center (TSC) in South Carolina recently feasted on this specially made soup with gusto.

“Pumpkin is a great seasonal addition for the turtles,” keeper Carly Sprott tells Popular Science. “It helps keep them hydrated, contains vitamins A and C, as well as fiber that aids in digestion. It is not something we would feed turtles as their entire meal very often, instead we offer balanced meals of fresh salads and various proteins depending on the species’ needs. They were absolutely thrilled when they received a taste of one of their favorite fall snacks!”

In the wild, Asian giant tortoises are found in tropical and subtropical mountainous evergreen forests in parts of Bangladesh and Indonesia. These freshwater turtles are listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List, and their primary threats are habitat destruction, collection for local consumption, and collection for pet and food trades. Freshwater turtles like these help their ecosystems by dispersing seeds after eating local plants, dig burrows that other animals in the area can use as shelter, and maintain some balance in the food chain. They also eat plenty of algae and invasive plants, which then improves water quality.

These particular Asian giant tortoises were the first turtles brought into the rescue center in 2013. They were taken from the wild legally in the 1990s, before there were stricter regulations regarding turtle conservation. While the team at the TSC does not name the hundreds of turtles living there, these three do have names since they were the center’s first turtles. They are named Emy-Sue, Emy-Jane, and Emy-Phay, which comes from the Asian giant tortoises’ scientific name—Manouria emys phayrei.

To make things fun, the team creates seasonal treats like these pumpkin soups. In the summer, they will hollow out watermelons. “They love to eat and always follow us around the enclosure to see if they will be awarded an extra treat,” Sprott says.

When they are not eating soup, they spend their days soaking in fresh water pools, warming underneath heat lamps, and roaming around in their large outdoor space.

The TSC is home to 27 turtle and tortoise species, including some of the world’s most endangered that need help.

“Currently, over half of all turtle species in the world are threatened with extinction. These captivating reptiles need our support,” says Sprott . “A few things the community can do to help include cleaning up litter that washes into waterways, supporting local conservation efforts, and treating wildlife with respect in their natural habitats.”

#4528. Tested: The 2027 BMW i7 60 xDrive Exemplifies EV Luxury

BMW’s largest executive sedan remains well suited to battery-electric power.

Taking a classic nameplate and turning it electric is a gamble for most automakers. For BMW, offering identical versions of the same model with gas-powered and all-electric powertrains has become a familiar formula. First launched in 2023, the BMW i7 has already earned plenty of love because of its smooth and silent demeanor. Can an all-new interior design philosophy cement its legacy?

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

The BMW i7’s core blueprint is unchanged for 2027, but the new front end is obvious at first glance. More handsome horizontal grille slats connect a still-oversized kidney grille, while extended LED taillights connect the rear end. Inside, the BMW i7 features an updated operating system, a sleek panoramic display, and a dose of Neue Klasse styling.

Powertrain layout: 1 rear electric motor, 1 front electric motor

The mission of an extended-wheelbase executive sedan is poise, and the BMW i7 succeeds at delivering a soothing experience. Yet, powered by a 112.5-kWh battery pack, the i7 60 xDrive is also plenty fast. With 536 horsepower and 549 lb-ft of torque on tap, the i7 60 xDrive offered a surprising punch of performance.

Acceleration was swift—my experience matching BMW’s claim of a 4.6-second 0 to 60 mph—yet also dignified. Using a rear-biased, dual-electric-motor setup, the i7 doled out power in a more linear fashion than most electric vehicles. Peak torque arrived instantly and offered a genuine punch off the line, but I appreciated the more subtle wave of urge available at half-throttle and higher speeds. It felt quick enough to escape an entourage of paparazzi, but not so fast that an executive would be jostled in the rear seat by acceleration. A piped-in, synthesized sound that accompanied hard acceleration was the only sonic nod to speed.

At 6000 pounds, the BMW i7 is heavy. Even with BMW’s full suite of adaptive chassis control systems, including full air suspension and active roll stabilization, the i7 displayed its weight while winding through Orange County’s Ortega Highway. Akin to my experience in BMW’s new iX5, the electric sedan behaved appropriately but was clearly making full use of its electronic dynamic aids. Turn-in was quick enough and the steering weighted up nicely, but I could feel the active roll stabilization fighting to keep the front end pointed the right way. Similarly, midcorner bumps tended to unsettle the rear end into a quickly corrected side step. Steering feel was nowhere to be found either. But in a modern BMW, that’s no surprise, sadly.

Open highway miles were the i7’s comfort zone during my drive. The same heft that made the i7 uncertain in the canyons aided a silken ride, even on California’s disjointed highways. Like the 740, the i7 can decouple its roll bars to reduce unwanted in-cabin movement at higher speeds, and the suspension trick worked well in practice. The i7 felt soft yet secure even at a rapid cruise. Similarly, the 126.6-inch-wheelbase sedan belied its size around town, maneuvering confidently into tight parking spots and narrow urban alleys thanks to standard rear-wheel steering.

Being an EV, regenerative braking did much of the work in slowing this beastly sedan. The mechanical hardware required a stiff stab of the pedal to adequately slow down the Bimmer. However, regeneration kept the three-ton sedan in check while descending, especially when switched into the Medium or High setting.

BMW claims the i7 60 xDrive can do around 350 miles on a single charge. While I didn’t get a chance to charge it, the i7 proved to be fairly efficient during my test drive, reporting a little over three miles per kWh. Even with a mix of highway driving, canyon carving, and suburban crawling, the i7 maintained that efficiency level with little fluctuation.

The 2027 BMW i7 exhibited its biggest upgrades inside. The Panoramic iDrive system is the core of the new Neue Klasse interiors. Gone are physical iDrive controls, instead replaced by a full touchscreen system, operating on a 17.9-inch central infotainment display. An optional recessed 14.6-inch passenger screen is also available for the 2027 model year.

The glamour of BMW’s new system is tempered by a responsive but busy user experience. BMW earns points for adding a scrolling volume control near the nub shifter, but everything else is manipulated through the central touchscreen. There was a permanent menu with obvious icons for climate control, vehicle settings, navigation, and media inputs, but pressing any of these icons only started a multi-step process. Adjusting drive dynamics or climate controls required sifting through multiple menus. Despite these gripes, the responsiveness of the system was rapid, and owners will get used to the navigation over time. Shortcut functions can also be created and assigned.

BMW’s new projected dashboard illuminated necessary information across a span of masked glass on the dashboard, and the placement was nearly perfect for me. The speedometer was placed directly in front of me, while navigation and other secondary information was projected to the right. My only tactile complaint was the oddly shaped M Sport steering wheel. It is better than the four-spoke option we’ve tested on other modern BMWs, but not by much.

My two-tone i7 60 xDrive was appointed with Black Merino leather seats that were heated, cooled, and massaging. The seating experience was comfortable, though a loud fan noise from the ventilated seats was exacerbated in the otherwise-quiet EV. The plush leather seats were generously wide, and the equipped Dolby Atmos system was sonically satisfying. Interior sound levels were exceptionally low, except for the occasional speaker-based acceleration blurt.

The electric luxury sedan is a fairly full market, but the BMW i7 sits at the top of the spectrum alongside the Porsche Taycan and Lucid Air. At a base price of $108,800 (in 50 xDrive form), the i7 meets Lucid and Porsche in the middle. The Taycan starts at $114,250 with significantly more dynamic performance but less interior space. A base Lucid Air is a mere $72,400. For those looking for the benefits of BMW’s new architecture, the all-new i3 sedan offers a sharper driving experience and better range for significant savings but at the sacrifice of the first-class cabin space.

Choosing between a gas-powered and electric 7-series is arguably the harder decision. Battery-electric powertrains suit the luxury-liner mission well, and the i7 offers more power than the currently available gasoline 7-series trims. Further muddying the water is a slim $8000 delta between the base model gas 7-series and a lightly appointed i7. Ultimately, the decision will likely come down to driving range and performance desires.

Adjustable regenerative braking forces can be difficult to get just right, but BMW’s three-prong approach is nearly perfect. BMW offers Low, Medium, and High settings, all of which have distinct levels of braking force, plus an adaptive setting that uses a forward-facing camera to actively adjust retardation levels for traffic conditions.
